title: The Tax Refund
intro: An email says the tax office owes you money. Who does not like a refund?
Tap anything that looks odd to sniff it closer. Pin what is suspicious, clear what is harmless.
When you are sure, decide what to do.

notify.text: You are eligible for a refund of ₹4,128

subject.text: You are eligible for a refund of ₹4,128

p.text: bank account number and the code on the back of your card

addr.label: Not an official address
addr.lens: The email comes from civic-revenue-portal.info. An official tax office uses its own government address.
addr.why: Look-alike or odd addresses are a warning sign. Check the part after the @.

link.label: Look-alike link
link.lens: The button goes to civic-revenue-portal.info/claim, not to an official site.
link.why: Never claim money through an email link. Go to the official website you already know.

bank.label: Asks for bank and card details
bank.lens: It wants your account number and the code on the back of your card.
bank.why: Getting a refund never requires your card code. That is for paying.

deadline.label: Deadline pressure
deadline.why: Real refunds do not vanish in a day.

threat.label: Threat of a penalty
threat.lens: It warns of a penalty if you do not claim.
threat.why: You cannot be penalised for not claiming a gift. A threat gives it away.

name.label: "Dear Taxpayer"
name.why: Many real emails use your name, but a generic hello alone is not proof of a scam.

owed.label: Sounds welcome
owed.why: Good news can still be a trap. What it asks you to do decides.

from.label: Official-sounding name
from.lens: The sender says Civic Revenue Portal.
from.why: A name is easy to copy. Look at the address and the ask.

subject.label: A precise amount
subject.why: A precise number looks real, but scammers choose precise numbers on purpose.

actions.label: Check my tax account on the official website I already know
Report it as phishing and delete it

trap.title: Civic Revenue Portal · Claim
trap.ask: Enter your bank account number and the code on the back of your card to receive ₹4,128.

block_report.line: Reported and deleted. The fake site was reported and taken down.

verify.line: The official tax website showed no refund and no message. The email was fake. Case cracked.

ignore.line: You stayed safe. But the same email is landing in thousands of other inboxes.

go_ahead.line: The page copied your account number and card code. No refund came, but money left your account.

what_if.go_ahead: Checking your tax account on the official site you already know would have shown no refund at all.
what_if.ignore: Reporting takes two taps and gets the fake site taken down.
what_if.verify: Checking was smart. Reporting the email as well protects other people.

golden_rule: Government offices do not email or text to ask for your bank details. Use the official website you already know.

quick_check.q: An email says the tax office owes you a refund and asks for your bank details through a button. What do you do?

options.text: Click it, it is your money
Reply to ask if it is real
Do not click. Check on the official website you already know, and report it

quick_check.explain: Government offices do not ask for your bank details by email or text. A refund never needs your card code.

hints.nudge: Look at the address the email really came from.

rows.v: A government website you already know

rows.k: Do government offices ask for money or details by email or text?

rows.v: Call or visit the official website on a number or address you know is correct
